messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marisol Alvarez was 61 when she finally came to treatment, a married bus driver who had spent most of her life in the same city routes, moving schoolchildren, shift workers, and elderly riders through neighborhoods she knew by heart. The event she could not shake had happened years earlier, on a wet afternoon when she was off duty but riding as a passenger behind a collision on a crowded road. She had watched two cars slam together at an intersection, metal folding in on itself, one driver thrown forward in a way that left Marisol staring at blood on the windshield and at the frightened faces of bystanders who seemed, for a few frozen seconds, unable to do anything. She remembered the shock of not being in control, the ugly scramble of people shouting, and her own helplessness as she stood there realizing that someone might not make it. Ever since, what should have faded into the past returned to her body as if it were still happening: at times the scene arrived with every sense at once, the smell of gasoline and wet asphalt, the sound of impact, the sight of blood, and her chest tightening before she could think. At other moments there was no clear picture at all, only the full force of terror and dread, as though the whole episode had erupted inside her without warning, and she would look around, disoriented, certain she was back at the roadside again.

In the months that followed, Marisol became convinced that the worst part of the day had not been the crash itself but her failure to stop it from becoming worse. She told herself, with a harshness that never let up, that she should have protected people and that she had done too little when it counted. Whenever a memory of the crash surfaced, it seemed to prove those thoughts all over again. She would be hit by the same vivid rush, feel the event as present rather than over, and immediately judge herself for her inaction, telling herself she would never forgive herself for not doing more. On other days, the memory came as an unbearable wave of emotion with no image attached, and that raw feeling only strengthened her belief that her life was no longer worth living in the way it had been. Certain sights made the shame flare again before she could get them under control: blood from a paper cut, a bent fender on the street, cars that had been hit by accident at an intersection. In those moments she felt the old panic and guilt surge together, as if the present scene had unlocked the original one and confirmed her failures.

To keep the terror and self-blame from taking over, Marisol developed a set of private rituals and prohibitions. She would sit alone before driving or leaving the house and repeat thoughts in her head over and over, trying to ward off another catastrophe by mentally preventing it, as if careful thinking might keep bad things from happening again. She also began avoiding any form of physical contact with others; even a reassuring touch from her husband could make her feel exposed and keyed up, as though her body had learned that contact was unsafe. Grief reminders were pushed away with equal determination. She skipped family photographs and changed the channel if a song reminded her of someone she had lost, because any such reminder seemed to bring the crash and all the losses around it back into the room with her. But the rituals never really soothed her. The more she tried to think her way out of danger, the more vividly the roadside scene seemed to return, and the more certain she became that she had already failed to protect anyone once and could fail again. That certainty made her scan for danger constantly, especially on her bus routes, where every sudden brake, scrape, or glimpse of blood on the sidewalk could turn into a trigger. She found herself tensing whenever cars were parked badly or when she had to pass an intersection with a history of accidents, and the route she once knew so well began to feel like a place full of warning signs.

Over time, the cost spread into daily life. Marisol became increasingly careful and withdrawn at home, keeping distance from her husband and making excuses when relatives reached for her arm. She noticed that her mental rituals left her exhausted and less present with passengers and coworkers, yet she felt unable to stop, because if she did not keep trying to prevent disaster in her mind, she feared the memory would break through again and prove that she had not done enough. Even on ordinary days, the memory could be stirred by the sight of blood on a scraped knee, by a crunch of metal in traffic, or by the feeling of being trapped and unable to control what was happening around her. Each time, the old scene came back with frightening immediacy, and each return deepened her conviction that she had failed, that she could not trust herself to protect others, and that her life had become smaller and less worth living. What finally brought Marisol in was that she had begun dreading the bus yard itself, where the parked cars, the close quarters, and the possibility of touching or being touched by coworkers all felt like too many reminders at once. She came because she was afraid that the next time the memory hit, she would be overwhelmed on the job, and because, beneath the shame, she still hoped there might be a way to stop living as though the crash were happening all over again.
